title: Why Airplane Windows Are Round (It Cost 56 Lives)

shots.vo: January, nineteen fifty-four. The most advanced airliner on Earth is climbing over the Mediterranean in perfect weather. Then, in a single second, it comes apart in the sky.
shots.prompt: wide shot, a 1950s silver four-engine jet airliner breaking apart in mid-air high above a calm blue Mediterranean sea, debris and smoke trails, distant view, clear daylight

shots.vo: Three months later, it happens again. Fifty-six people are dead, and nobody can explain why.
shots.prompt: interior, empty 1950s airliner passenger cabin, rows of vintage seats, sunlight beams through square windows, dust in the air, no people

shots.vo: The answer was hiding in plain sight. In fact, it is right next to you, every time you fly.
shots.prompt: over-the-shoulder view from a modern airplane seat, oval cabin window with rounded corners, airplane wing outside above white clouds

shots.vo: By the end of this video, you will never look at an airplane window the same way again.
shots.prompt: close-up, a single oval airplane window with rounded corners inside a dark cabin, one beam of light shining through

shots.vo: Look at any airliner window. A soft oval. No sharp corners. Not one, on any passenger jet flying today.
shots.prompt: interior, a row of oval windows along the wall of a modern airliner cabin, soft warm reading lights, empty seats

shots.vo: Most people think it is about style, or the view. The truth is darker. That shape was paid for with lives.
shots.prompt: back view silhouette of a traveler with headphones looking out of an oval airplane window at clouds, face not visible

shots.vo: To understand how, we have to go back to the first jet airliner the world ever built. A plane years ahead of anything else in the sky.
shots.prompt: 1950s silver jet airliner parked on an empty airfield at dawn, four engines inside the wings, long row of large square windows on the fuselage, low angle

shots.vo: May, nineteen fifty-two. The de Havilland Comet carries its first paying passengers. For a moment, Britain owns the future of flight.
shots.prompt: 1950s silver jet airliner taking off from a runway, crowd of people in 1950s coats watching behind a wire fence, morning

shots.vo: It flies almost twice as high as the propeller planes of its day, above the weather. Smooth. Quiet. Fast. Passengers have never felt anything like it.
To keep people alive that high, air is pumped into the cabin until the whole fuselage swells like a balloon. Remember that. It matters.
And along its sides runs a row of big, almost square windows. Passengers love them. Engineers are proud of them.
shots.prompt: interior, 1950s jet airliner cabin, large almost square windows, passengers in 1950s suits and hats seated, soft focus faces, warm light

shots.vo: Then, on the tenth of January, nineteen fifty-four, B. O. A. C. Flight seven eight one climbs out of Rome, bound for London.
shots.prompt: 1950s silver jet airliner climbing over the Italian coast in morning light, the city of Rome far below, aerial view

shots.vo: Near the island of Elba, it breaks apart in the air. All thirty-five people on board are lost.
shots.prompt: aerial view of the island of Elba in a calm turquoise sea, a thin trail of smoke in an empty sky above it, somber

shots.vo: Fishermen below watch the pieces fall into the sea.
shots.prompt: 1950s Italian wooden fishing boats on a calm sea, fishermen standing in the boats looking up at the sky, seen from behind

shots.vo: The Comets are grounded. Investigators suspect a fire, or an engine. Changes are made, and within weeks the jets are flying again. That decision would cost twenty-one more lives.
shots.prompt: 1950s aircraft engineers in overalls inspecting an open jet engine bay inside a hangar, work lamps, toolboxes

shots.vo: On the eighth of April, South African Airways Flight two oh one leaves Rome for Cairo.
shots.prompt: 1950s silver jet airliner climbing into an orange evening sky over the coast of southern Italy, side view

shots.vo: Near Naples, it vanishes from the sky. Twenty-one more people are gone.
shots.prompt: the Bay of Naples at dusk, Mount Vesuvius on the horizon, an empty darkening sky, still water, haunting mood

shots.vo: Two identical aircraft. Two clear days. No storm. No bomb. No pilot error anyone can find. So what is tearing these planes apart?
The world's most modern airliner is taken out of service, and Britain launches one of the biggest crash investigations in history.
shots.prompt: high angle, 1950s investigation hall, long tables covered with twisted aluminium wreckage, investigators in suits and white lab coats

shots.vo: The Royal Navy searches the seabed off Elba, and lifts piece after piece of the first Comet from the water.
shots.prompt: 1950s Royal Navy salvage ship at sea, a crane lifting a twisted piece of metal fuselage out of the water, grey sky

shots.vo: At Farnborough, the fragments are laid out and rebuilt like a giant puzzle. But the most important piece is still missing.
shots.prompt: inside a huge hangar, reassembled wreckage of a silver airliner fuselage on a wooden frame, missing pieces, engineers with clipboards

shots.vo: The wreckage cannot show what happened in the air. So the investigators try something nobody has ever done.
shots.prompt: inside a hangar, a complete silver 1950s airliner fuselage being lowered by cranes into a giant rectangular water tank

shots.vo: They put an entire Comet into a giant tank of water, and they fly it, over and over, without it ever leaving the ground.
shots.prompt: a 1950s airliner fuselage submerged in a massive water tank, pipes and pumps around it, engineers watching from a walkway

shots.vo: Water is pumped into the cabin to stretch it, exactly like a flight at cruising height. Then released. Then again. Every cycle is one flight.
Day and night, the tank keeps flying. And after about three thousand flights' worth of cycles, the fuselage splits open.
shots.prompt: underwater inside a giant test tank, a long jagged split tearing open the riveted aluminium skin of an airliner fuselage, bubbles escaping, dramatic light

shots.vo: The crack starts at a corner. The sharp corner of a squarish opening in the skin.
shots.prompt: extreme close-up of a flat riveted aluminium panel with one square window cut-out, a single thin dark crack running diagonally away from its sharp top corner, rows of rivets, studio light
shots.negative: airplane, aircraft, jet, wing, fuselage, holes, rust, organic, leaf, mud, skin

shots.vo: Here is what they found. When the cabin swells, the metal around every opening is pulled tight. Around a smooth curve, that pull flows evenly.
But at a sharp corner, it piles up into one tiny point. Right there, the metal is pulled far harder than anywhere else.
Every flight stretches that point a little. Not enough to break. Just enough to tire it.
Engineers call it metal fatigue. Invisible cracks grow, flight after flight, until one day the skin simply lets go.
shots.prompt: macro close-up of a smooth polished aluminium sheet with neat rows of rivets, a hairline fatigue crack spreading from one rivet hole across the metal, cold metallic light
shots.negative: airplane, aircraft, jet, wing, fuselage, holes, rust, organic, leaf, mud, skin

shots.vo: And when a pressurised cabin fails at thirty thousand feet, it does not leak. It bursts.
shots.prompt: high above white clouds, the silver fuselage of a 1950s jet airliner bursting open along its side, a sudden white cloud of vapour and fragments, wide distant view, not graphic

shots.vo: Later, a section of the Elba Comet's roof is pulled from the sea. The break had started at the corner of a small square opening. Exactly as the tank predicted.
shots.prompt: a piece of salvaged silver aircraft roof panel on a wooden workbench, a small square hole cut in the metal with one corner torn open, rivet rows, a desk lamp, investigators' tools
shots.negative: holes, rust, organic, leather, cloth, green

shots.vo: The lesson rewrote the rules of aviation. When the Comet returned in a new version, its windows were oval.
shots.prompt: 1950s-style silver jet airliner with oval windows flying above sunlit clouds, hopeful bright mood, side view

shots.vo: Today every airliner on Earth has windows with rounded corners, so the stress flows around them instead of piling up in one place.
Right now, thousands of cabins above you are swelling a little on every flight, and shrinking again when they land.
shots.prompt: modern passenger jet at an airport gate at night, cabin lights glowing through its row of oval windows, wet tarmac reflections

shots.vo: They survive, because of what those investigators learned in nineteen fifty-four.
shots.prompt: inside a modern airplane, close-up of the rounded corner of a cabin window frame, the engine and wing visible outside, soft light

shots.vo: So the next time you lean against that little oval window, remember the fifty-six people who gave it its shape.
shots.prompt: a child's small hand touching an oval airplane window, sunset clouds outside, warm amber light

shots.vo: And that is the hidden why.
shots.prompt: a single oval airplane window glowing in a completely dark cabin, centered, quiet
